claims.text: The target material is single-phase FCC CoCrFeMnNi.
Adding high-resolution grain-size, grain-boundary-density, and lattice-distortion descriptors to an advanced machine-learning model will improve predictions of phonon thermal conductivity.
The microstructure-informed model will predict phonon thermal conductivity values that are 20–30% lower than values predicted by composition-only models.
Predictions that are 20–30% lower will be more accurate for low-conductivity materials.
Severe plastic deformation followed by controlled annealing under ultra-high vacuum will produce an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer in CoCrFeMnNi.
TEM/STEM can provide grain-size, grain-boundary-density, and lattice-distortion descriptors for the model.
The ultra-nanocrystalline layer increases grain-boundary density.
Grain boundaries act as effective phonon-scattering centers.
Increased grain-boundary density and local lattice distortions enhance phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering lowers the phonon mean free path.
A model incorporating microstructural descriptors can capture scattering phenomena neglected by composition-only empirical approaches.
Experimental measurements will show an approximately 20–30% reduction in thermal conductivity relative to composition- and bulk-property-based predictions.
The microstructure-informed model will achieve a statistically significant improvement in cross-validated predictive accuracy over conventional models.
The predictive improvement applies to CoCrFeMnNi and other high-entropy alloys subjected to controlled grain refinement.
Noisy microstructural data or failure to produce a uniform ultra-nanocrystalline structure may eliminate the predictive improvement.
Model performance depends critically on the quality and consistency of the microstructural dataset.
Laser flash analysis can provide the phonon thermal conductivity needed to test the hypothesis over a range of temperatures.

The hypothesis is to be falsified if confirmed ultra-nanocrystalline samples do not exhibit a 20–30% reduction relative to conventional predictions or if the new model does not statistically outperform existing methods.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis equates a 20–30% lower numerical prediction with improved predictive accuracy, whereas the outcome and falsification rule treat a 20–30% difference between measurement and conventional prediction as a physical conductivity reduction. A lower prediction is not inherently a smaller prediction error, so the claimed model improvement and the physical effect are conflated.
